cards.stem: Read the article and answer the questions which follow. Natural Capital and Other Resources Agriculture is the world’s largest user of freshwater, accounting for 70% of global freshwater use. There are large differences in water use between regions and farming systems. In more temperate regions like Ireland, the interface between agriculture and water is predominantly defined by the impact of farming on the quality of drinking and surface waters. cards.stem: Read the article and answer the questions which follow. Chewing Cud: Signs of Rumination in Cows Every farmer, stockperson and veterinarian know that animals resting and chewing the cud are healthy and making them profit. Chewing the cud is the key visible sign of ruminant livestock health and wellbeing. There are many factors that may influence the amount of time an animal spends chewing the cud, for example: Time of feeding – cows tend to eat more at dusk compared to dawn and hence ruminating more at night; feed space – if restricted, cows spending more time foraging for food; forage chop length and its correlation between fibre and starch/sugar – can account for up to a 33% of the variation in the time spent chewing. (Adapted from Agriland, 2022) [The term underlined on the paper is: Chewing the cud]

rows.text: When a portion of food returns from a ruminant’s stomach to the mouth, to be re-chewed.

cards.question: Explain the relationship between nutrient availability in soil and cation exchange capacity in soils.

rows.text: As CEC increases, more nutrients are attached to soil particles, and fewer remain in the soil solution / since the nutrients in soil solution are available to plants, this means that while there are plenty of nutrients in the soil, the plants may not be able to take advantage of them.

cards.question: Describe an investigation to demonstrate cation exchange capacity in a sample of soil.

texts: Add (high pH) soil to filter paper in a funnel with a clean dry beaker underneath
add potassium chloride (or potassium ions) solution (drop by drop) to the soil
collect the water that filters from the soil into the beaker (leachate)
test the leachate for calcium by adding (10 drops) ammonium oxalate to the leachate
white precipitate forms, calcium is present
discard the leachate and rinse the beaker with deionised water
repeat the experiment by adding more potassium chloride to the soil and testing the leachate for calcium
repeat the experiment until the leachate does not test positive for calcium
rows.note: Three points from one coherent investigation, 3(4).

cards.question: Briefly explain each of the following in relation to the soil.

rows.text: Field capacity: is the amount of soil moisture or water content held in soil after excess water has drained away
Poaching: loss of soils by the damaging action of feet of livestock or machinery which can negatively affect availability of productive land and soil structure
Flocculation: process during which particles of a soil, dispersed in a solution contact and adhere each another, forming clusters, flocks, flakes, or clumps of a larger size.
Microbiome: is a reversible process in which the cations are exchanged or interchanged between the solid and liquid phases or between the solid and solid phases when they come in close contact
rows.note: Microbiome. The scheme prints 4(4), one explanation for each term. See the source note: this printed answer describes cation exchange, not the soil microbiome.
